hooks.text: The Moon's brightest rocks are too young to exist.
Why did a single bright moon rock shatter lunar science?
A glowing white moon rock shattered our lunar history.

title: The Moon Rock That Broke Lunar History
description: Apollo astronauts returned with bright lunar rocks that challenged everything we thought we knew about the Moon's ancient magma ocean.

beats.text: The Moon's brightest rocks are too young to exist.
beats.visual: Apollo photograph of the bright lunar highlands on the far side of the Moon, 1972

beats.text: Apollo astronauts brought back samples of anorthosite, a highly reflective, coarse-grained rock covering the lunar highlands.
beats.visual: Apollo 15 photograph of lunar Sample 15415, the Genesis Rock, 1971

beats.text: Scientists believed the entire Moon once had a global magma ocean, where these light crystals floated to the top.
beats.visual: Artist's illustration of the early Moon covered in a global magma ocean

beats.text: To study this primordial crust, geologists compared it to similar rock deposits in Canada and Scandinavia.
beats.visual: Aerial photograph of mountain peaks in Norway, 2020

beats.text: But a 2011 study re-dated lunar Sample 60025 to just 4.36 billion years old.
beats.visual: Close-up photograph of Apollo lunar sample 60025 in a sterile laboratory

beats.text: This young age shattered the theory of a single, rapidly cooling global magma ocean.
beats.visual: Artist's illustration of a giant asteroid impact bombarding the early Moon

beats.text: Now, scientists are debating whether the Moon's crust actually built up slowly through multiple volcanic episodes.
beats.visual: Scientific diagram of fractional crystallization inside an active magma chamber

beats.text: To solve how planets form, we first have to explain why the Moon's brightest rocks are too young to exist.
beats.visual: Apollo 16 photograph of John Young collecting lunar samples on the Moon, 1972
